title: Week 1: Getting Set Up

Key Concepts

A website needs files, usually HTML, and a server that makes those files available online.
Quarto converts .qmd source files into .html pages.
Saving a source file, rendering a site, committing a snapshot, and pushing to GitHub are separate actions.
A .qmd file can combine YAML metadata, Markdown writing, executable R code, and rendered results.
Source files are edited by people; output and cache files are generated by tools.

dplyr, an R package for transforming tables.
tidycensus, an R package for downloading Census and American Community Survey (ACS) data.

The class connected data manipulation with an important data source: Census geography and ACS estimates.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Key Concepts

An object stores a value or a table in R.
A function takes an input, performs an operation, and returns an output.
A tibble is a modern data frame: observations are rows and variables are columns.
dplyr verbs make table operations readable: filter rows, select columns, create variables, sort rows, and summarize groups.
The Decennial Census is a full population count every ten years; the ACS is a continuous sample survey that publishes estimates with margins of error.
A GEOID is a geographic identifier and should be stored as text so leading zeros are preserved.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at the number with a bachelor’s degree across counties in New York State, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                        estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                          <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Hamilton County, New York        586    99   16.9 
 2 Schuyler County, New York       1570   206   13.1 
 3 Yates County, New York          2427   269   11.1 
 4 Essex County, New York          4885   541   11.1 
 5 Fulton County, New York         5111   541   10.6 
 6 Sullivan County, New York       9476   986   10.4 
 7 Montgomery County, New York     3888   400   10.3 
 8 Washington County, New York     5649   573   10.1

10 Lewis County, New York          2060   203    9.85

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 36001 Albany County, New York       49653   1534  315374    NA
2 36003 Allegany County, New York      3787    306   47027    NA
3 36005 Bronx County, New York       130281   3296 1419250    NA
4 36007 Broome County, New York       21526   1008  197738    NA
5 36009 Cattaraugus County, New York   6055    387   76479    NA
6 36011 Cayuga County, New York        7436    457   75464    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         24        730694.
2 Low confidence           8         40855.
3 Moderate                30         66961.


The 24 high-confidence counties have an average population of approximately 730,694, compared with 66,961 for the 30 moderate-confidence counties and 40,855 for the 8 low-confidence counties. This pattern suggests that more populous counties tend to have more reliable ACS estimates, while smaller counties tend to have larger margins of error relative to their estimates.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
Among all the counties in New York State, Hamilton County has the least reliable estimate: 586 residents aged 25 or older were estimated to have a bachelor’s degree as their highest level of education, with a margin of error of 99, or 16.9% of the estimate. Schuyler County follows with a relative margin of error of 13.1%, while Yates and Essex Counties are both about 11.1%. Overall, eight counties fall into the low-confidence category.
This reflects how the American Community Survey (ACS) works. The ACS estimates population characteristics from a sample rather than counting every resident. Smaller counties contribute fewer sampled households and residents, so each response carries more weight and the estimates have greater uncertainty. In this analysis, low-confidence counties have an average population of 40,855, compared with 730,694 in high-confidence counties.
Ignoring this margin of error might lead to unfair policy decisions. If a state agency directed workforce-development funding toward counties with fewer bachelor’s degree holders, it might treat every county estimate as equally precise. If a small county’s bachelor’s degree count were overestimated, it could appear better educated and receive less support than it needs as the result. Rural counties such as Hamilton, Schuyler, and Yates are especially vulnerable because their limited sample sizes make their estimates less stable. Agencies should consider margins of error and avoid making funding decisions based on small differences alone.

  <chr>                        <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>

This comparison shows that ACS estimates become much less precise at smaller geographic scales because each tract is represented by a smaller sample.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Notes

1. Objects, functions, arguments, and comments
This example keeps counties with populations above 50,000 and stores the result in a new object:
result <- filter(counties, population > 50000) # Keep larger counties

result is the object that stores the output.
<- is the assignment operator.
filter() is the function.
counties is the input data.
population > 50000 is an argument or condition.
Text after # is a comment and is not executed.

R is case-sensitive, so result and Result are different objects. Using lowercase object and function names consistently prevents avoidable errors.


2. Packages: install once, load each session
A package is a collection of functions. Installation happens once on a computer; loading happens at the start of each new R session.
# Run once on a computer
install.packages("dplyr")
install.packages("tidycensus")

# Run in each new R session
library(dplyr)
library(tidycensus)
I think of install.packages() as putting a book on the shelf and library() as taking that book off the shelf to use it.


3. Tibbles and dplyr verbs
A tibble is a table in which each row is an observation and each column is a variable.



NAME
INCOME
MOE




Adams
78,975
1,237


Berks
74,617
4,372


Bucks
104,200
2,374



Common dplyr verbs:

filter() keeps rows that meet a condition.
select() keeps or reorders columns.
mutate() adds or changes a computed column.
arrange() changes row order; desc() requests descending order.
group_by() and summarize() turn many rows into group-level summaries.

A correct mutate() expression must name the new column:
counties <- counties |>
  mutate(income_doubled = income * 2)
The same sequence of operations can be written step by step:
step_1 <- filter(counties, moe_pct > 10)
step_2 <- arrange(step_1, desc(moe_pct))
step_3 <- select(step_2, NAME, moe_pct)
Or as one pipeline. Both %>% and the base-R pipe |> mean roughly “and then.”
new_data <- counties |>
  filter(moe_pct > 10) |>
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) |>
  select(NAME, moe_pct)
Grouping allows us to calculate one value for each category:
county_income |>
  group_by(STATE) |>
  summarize(min_income = min(INCOME))


4. Decennial Census and the ACS
The two Census Bureau products answer different questions:








Product
What it provides
Important limitation




Decennial Census
A full population count every 10 years, down to Census blocks
Limited social and economic characteristics


American Community Survey
Ongoing sample-based estimates for income, education, housing, commuting, and more
Every estimate includes uncertainty



Important ACS products:

ACS 1-year: more current, but available only for areas with populations of 65,000 or more.
ACS 5-year: combines five years of responses, covers small geographies, and is generally more precise for tract or block-group analysis.
ACS 3-year: discontinued after the 2013 release.

For ACS data, always keep two values in mind:
Estimate (E)        the estimated value
Margin of Error (M) the uncertainty around that estimate


5. Census geography and GEOIDs
The basic geographic hierarchy is:
state -> county -> Census tract -> block group -> Census block
Census tract boundaries can change over time. Block groups are available in ACS 5-year data, but their smaller samples often produce large margins of error, so they should be used cautiously rather than rejected automatically. Census blocks are primarily associated with Decennial Census data.
A tract GEOID has 11 digits. For example:
42101000100
42     = Pennsylvania state FIPS
101    = Philadelphia County FIPS
000100 = Census tract code
GEOIDs are identifiers, not quantities, so they should be stored as character strings:
geoid <- "42101000100"


6. ACS variable codes and tidycensus
In the raw ACS name B19013_001E:

B19013 is the table number.
001 is the line number.
E means estimate; M means margin of error.

When using tidycensus, the variable is normally requested without the final E or M:
library(tidycensus)

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(
    median_income = "B19013_001",
    total_population = "B01003_001"
  ),
  state = "PA",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)


7. Long and wide data

Long (tidy) output: one geography-variable combination per row, with variable, estimate, and moe columns.
Wide output: one geographic unit per row, with separate estimate and MOE columns such as median_incomeE and median_incomeM.

Long format is useful for repeated operations across variables; wide format is often convenient for comparison, modeling, and joins.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
Notes

1. What is a website?
In the class workflow, a website has two main parts:
a folder of HTML files + a server that is always online
For this portfolio:
Quarto creates the HTML files
GitHub Pages hosts those files online
The complete path from source to website is:
.qmd source file -> Quarto Render -> .html page -> GitHub Pages
I normally edit the .qmd source rather than the generated .html file.


2. Quarto and Render
Quarto is a publishing system that combines writing, code, and results in one document. It can render a .qmd file as a webpage, PDF, slide deck, or Word document.
When I select Render, Quarto:

Reads the .qmd file from top to bottom.
Finds executable code chunks.
Sends R code to R and receives the results.
Combines the writing, code, and output into HTML.

Saving only records edits in the source file. Rendering rebuilds the output page, so Save is not Render.


3. Anatomy of a .qmd file
A Quarto document normally contains three parts:
YAML header + Markdown text + R code chunks

YAML header
The YAML header goes at the very top and stores page metadata:
---
title: "Week 1: Getting Set Up"
description: "My first weekly note"
date: 2026-08-28
---
Important YAML rules:

The opening and closing --- lines matter.
A colon must be followed by a space.
Dates should use YYYY-MM-DD.
Use plain quotation marks.



Markdown
Markdown provides headings, paragraphs, lists, emphasis, and links:
## What I Learned

This is a paragraph with a [link](https://quarto.org/).

- First point
- Second point


R code chunks
An executable R chunk in a Quarto file uses an opening fence labeled {r}. The code inside a chunk might look like this:
library(tidycensus)

x <- 2 + 2
print(x)
R code should be placed inside a code chunk when I want Quarto to run it and include the result in the page.



4. Files and folders
A useful question is: Who is this file for?
Files I edit directly:
index.qmd
about.qmd
weekly-notes/*.qmd
assignments/*.qmd
_quarto.yml
Files and folders mainly used by software:







Item
Purpose




.Rproj
Opens the folder as an RStudio project


.gitignore
Tells Git which files not to track


.Renviron
Stores environment variables and secrets such as API keys


docs/
Contains the rendered website published by GitHub Pages


_freeze/
Stores Quarto execution results and cache data



The key rule is: edit source files and allow Quarto to regenerate output files.


5. Why index.qmd matters
Web servers normally look for index.html when a visitor requests a folder URL. Quarto creates that file from index.qmd:
index.qmd -> Render -> docs/index.html
That is why the portfolio homepage source file is named index.qmd.


6. Git, GitHub.com, and GitHub Desktop
These tools are related but have different roles:

Git is the version-control system running locally on my computer.
GitHub.com stores an online copy of the repository.
GitHub Desktop provides buttons and menus that send commands to Git.

Commit and push are also different:
Commit = save a labeled snapshot in the local Git repository
Push   = send local commits to GitHub.com


7. The portfolio workflow
Edit -> Save -> Render -> Commit -> Push -> wait -> refresh the live site
Each step changes a different version of the work:

Edit and Save: update the local source file.
Render: rebuild the local website output.
Commit: record a labeled local snapshot.
Push: transfer commits to GitHub.com.
Refresh: check the published GitHub Pages site.



8. Markdown, R scripts, and Quarto documents
Markdown text = writing and formatting, without calculation
R script      = reusable code
.qmd document = writing + code + results
An R script is useful for experimenting with code and building reusable analysis. A .qmd document is useful when I need to explain the analysis and publish its results together.

title: Assignment 3：Verify the Claim of Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 2: Test

Poverty rates and margins of error
Because the poverty rate is a proportion, I calculate its 90% margin of error with moe_prop().


Show code
poverty_2010 <- poverty_2010 %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate = below_povertyE / totalE,
    poverty_rate_moe = moe_prop(
      num = below_povertyE,
      denom = totalE,
      moe_num = below_povertyM,
      moe_denom = totalM
    )
  )

poverty_2017 <- poverty_2017 %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate = below_povertyE / totalE,
    poverty_rate_moe = moe_prop(
      num = below_povertyE,
      denom = totalE,
      moe_num = below_povertyM,
      moe_denom = totalM
    )
  )




Missing values
First I check 2006–2010 for zero denominators or missing estimates.


Show code
missing_2010 <- poverty_2010 %>%
  filter(
    totalE == 0 |
      is.na(poverty_rate) |
      is.na(poverty_rate_moe)
  )

dim(missing_2010)


[1] 7 8


dim() reports rows, then columns. The seven rows are tracts with no valid 2006–2010 rate.
The same check for 2013–2017 gives:


Show code
missing_2017 <- poverty_2017 %>%
  filter(
    totalE == 0 |
      is.na(poverty_rate) |
      is.na(poverty_rate_moe)
  )

dim(missing_2017)


[1] 8 8


Eight tracts have no valid 2013–2017 rate. In both periods, invalid rates come from zero denominators, so I exclude them rather than treat them as zero. Matching leaves 376 usable tracts.


Reliability
I calculate CV as (MOE / 1.645) / poverty rate * 100. Following Jurjevich et al. (2018), CV below 12% is High confidence, 12–40% is Moderate, and above 40% is Low confidence.


Show code
poverty_2010_valid <- poverty_2010 %>%
  filter(
    totalE > 0,
    !is.na(poverty_rate),
    !is.na(poverty_rate_moe)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    period = "2006–2010",
    poverty_rate_se = poverty_rate_moe / 1.645,
    cv = poverty_rate_se / poverty_rate * 100,
    reliability = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "High confidence",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Moderate",
      TRUE     ~ "Low confidence"
    )
  )

poverty_2017_valid <- poverty_2017 %>%
  filter(
    totalE > 0,
    !is.na(poverty_rate),
    !is.na(poverty_rate_moe)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    period = "2013–2017",
    poverty_rate_se = poverty_rate_moe / 1.645,
    cv = poverty_rate_se / poverty_rate * 100,
    reliability = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "High confidence",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Moderate",
      TRUE     ~ "Low confidence"
    )
  )

city_rate_2017 <- sum(poverty_2017_valid$below_povertyE) /
  sum(poverty_2017_valid$totalE)

poverty_2010_valid %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_tracts = n()
  ) %>%

Most estimates are Moderate: 321 in 2006–2010 and 332 in 2013–2017. High-confidence counts are 11 and 22; low-confidence counts are 45 and 22.



Change between periods


Show code
poverty_wide <- bind_rows(
  poverty_2010_valid,
  poverty_2017_valid
) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, period, poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = period,
    values_from = c(poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe)
  )

poverty_tested <- poverty_wide %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(`poverty_rate_2006–2010`),
    !is.na(`poverty_rate_2013–2017`)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    change = `poverty_rate_2013–2017` - `poverty_rate_2006–2010`,
    se_1 = `poverty_rate_moe_2006–2010` / 1.645,
    se_2 = `poverty_rate_moe_2013–2017` / 1.645,
    se_diff = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645,
    result = case_when(
      significant & change > 0 ~ "Significant increase",
      significant & change < 0 ~ "Significant decrease",
      TRUE ~ "Not statistically detectable"
    )
  )

change_counts <- poverty_tested %>%
  count(result)




Show code
ggplot(change_counts, aes(x = result, y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Results of the tract-level change test",
    subtitle = "Individual 90% tests for 376 matched Philadelphia census tracts",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of tracts",
    caption = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau, ACS five-year estimates."
  )





Most Philadelphia tracts did not have a statistically detectable change in poverty rate.






Error-bar visualization
The figure shows the 20 largest detectable changes; the counts above include all 376 tracts.


Show code
change_plot_data <- poverty_tested %>%
  filter(significant) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(change))) %>%
  slice_head(n = 20) %>%
  mutate(
    NAME = str_remove(NAME, ", Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania"),
    change_pp = change * 100,
    moe_diff_pp = moe_diff * 100,
    direction = case_when(
      change > 0 ~ "Increase",
      TRUE ~ "Decrease"
    )
  )

change_plot_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, change_pp), y = change_pp)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = direction)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = change_pp - moe_diff_pp,
                    ymax = change_pp + moe_diff_pp), width = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Largest statistically detectable changes in poverty rate",
    subtitle = "Twenty largest absolute tract changes, 2006–2010 vs. 2013–2017",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Change in poverty rate (percentage points)",
    fill = NULL,
    caption = "Error bars show 90% margins of error; dashed line marks no change. Source: U.S. Census Bureau ACS."
  )





Largest statistically detectable tract-level changes in poverty rates, with 90% margins of error.




At 90% confidence, 63 of 376 tracts changed detectably: 36 increased and 27 decreased; 313 showed no detectable change. Poverty change was therefore uneven.

text:
Part 3: Adjudicate
Supported. Combining the tract counts gives a 2013–2017 city poverty rate of 25.8%, consistent with the article’s 26% figure. Poverty also increased in some places: 36 of 376 tracts show detectable increases. Not supported as a tract-level generalization. The increase was not widespread: 313 tracts show no detectable change and 27 show decreases.
Cannot be determined. The Fairhill, Eastwick, and Holmesburg figures cannot be reproduced because the article does not provide its tract-to-neighborhood crosswalk; the Holmesburg claim also requires race-specific data. Explanations involving opioids, migration, or displacement are beyond what these ACS estimates can establish.

title: Assignment 3：Verify the Claim of Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 4: Rewrite

Philadelphia’s poverty rate was about 25.8% in the 2013–2017 ACS. Change within the city was uneven: of 376 comparable census tracts, 36 had detectable increases, 27 had detectable decreases, and 313 had no detectable change at 90% confidence. Poverty worsened in some places, but not as a widespread tract-level pattern. The reported Fairhill, Eastwick, and Holmesburg figures cannot be reproduced because the article did not publish its tract-to-neighborhood crosswalk. The Holmesburg claim also requires race-specific poverty data.

section: Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
text:
Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
Build a half-mile zone around every station and merge the circles into one shape. Remember your units.

station_zone <- stations %>%
  st_buffer(dist = 0.5*5280) %>%
  st_union()

Pick whole cookies: which tracts don’t touch the zone at all?

outside_zone <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_filter(station_zone, .predicate = st_disjoint)

nrow(outside_zone)

[1] 162


Cut the dough: what share of each tract’s area falls inside the zone?

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(tract_area = as.numeric(st_area(.)))

covered <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_intersection(station_zone) %>%
  mutate(covered_area = as.numeric(st_area(.))) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(GEOID, covered_area)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  left_join(covered, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(pct_covered = replace_na(covered_area / tract_area, 0) * 100)

Notice: that last step is the left_join() from Part 1b. It’s a join by what (GEOID), used to bring a join-by-where result back into the table. The two kinds of join work together.

Part 2: Look before you model
The Week 3 habit comes first: plot the relationship before you fit anything.

ggplot(tracts, aes(x = med_incE, y = med_rentE)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +

Stop and look: Does a straight line describe this cloud well everywhere, or does it bend? Where are the points that sit far from the line?
The relationship is strongly positive but not perfectly linear: it starts to flatten among the highest-income tracts. A few low- and middle-income tracts have rents far above the line, and one very high-income tract has rent far below it.

Look at the n_stations coefficient. Answer both questions in one or two sentences each:

β̂ reading: Can you tell the housing agency that bike share stations raise rents? Why or why not?
Your answer: No. Holding the included variables constant, one additional nearby station is associated with about $5.48 higher monthly rent, but this observational coefficient does not establish causation. Stations may be placed in already-expensive, amenity-rich areas, and omitted neighborhood characteristics or reverse causality can explain the association.

text:
Part 5: Uncertainty in input data
Our Y is an ACS estimate with its own margin of error. Add the residuals to the table and check whether the biggest misses happen where the estimate is least reliable.

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(fitted_m2 = fitted(m2),
         resid_m2  = residuals(m2))

ggplot(tracts, aes(x = rent_cv, y = abs(resid_m2))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "CV of the median rent estimate (%)",
       y = "Size of the model's miss ($)",
       title = "Are the biggest misses in the noisiest tracts?") +
  theme_minimal()








Stop and look: If a tract’s rent estimate has a CV of 35%, how much of the model’s miss there could be survey noise rather than a model failure? What does that mean for flagging “tracts with rents above expectation”?
A 35% rent CV means the standard error is 35% of the estimate, so the ACS 90% margin of error is about \(1.645 \times 35\% = 57.6\%\) of the reported rent. A large share—and potentially all—of an apparent residual could therefore be sampling noise. The agency should attach reliability information to every flag and verify high-CV tracts before acting.

title: Week 5 In-Class Lab: Where the Model Is Wrong
text:
Part 6: Fit vs. prediction






WarningTwo different CVs



Week 3 CV = coefficient of variation: how noisy is one estimate? Today’s CV = cross-validation: how well does a model predict data it hasn’t seen? Same letters, unrelated ideas.



6A: One train/test split

set.seed(5080)
n <- nrow(tracts)
train_idx <- sample(1:n, size = 0.8 * n)

train_data <- tracts[train_idx, ]
test_data  <- tracts[-train_idx, ]

m2_train <- lm(med_rentE ~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations,
               data = train_data)

test_pred <- predict(m2_train, newdata = test_data)

rmse_train <- sqrt(mean(residuals(m2_train)^2))
rmse_test  <- sqrt(mean((test_data$med_rentE - test_pred)^2))

c(train = rmse_train, test = rmse_test)

   train     test 
252.6854 265.7514 


Stop and look: Which RMSE is larger? Why would you expect that? In words: “The model’s typical miss on tracts it hasn’t seen is about $266 per month.”
The test RMSE ($265.75) is larger than the training RMSE ($252.69), as expected because the model was optimized on the training observations. The model’s typical miss on tracts it has not seen is about $266 per month for this split.
Change the seed to any other number and rerun the chunk. Did the test RMSE change? That’s why one split isn’t enough.


6B: 10-fold cross-validation
caret wants a plain data frame, so drop the geometry first. (The geometry isn’t a predictor, and train() will choke on it.)

model_df <- tracts %>% st_drop_geometry()

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

set.seed(5080)
cv_m1 <- train(med_rentE ~ med_incE,
               data = model_df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)

set.seed(5080)

Part 7: Where is the model wrong?

7A: Residuals vs. fitted

ggplot(tracts, aes(x = fitted_m2, y = resid_m2)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red") +
  labs(x = "Predicted rent", y = "Residual (actual − predicted)") +
  theme_minimal()

    studentized Breusch-Pagan test

data:  m2
BP = 13.807, df = 4, p-value = 0.007938


Stop and look: Random cloud, funnel, or curve? If it’s a funnel, the predictions aren’t biased, but one RMSE hides the fact that the model misses by much more in some tracts. Which tracts?
The plot is closer to a funnel than a random cloud: residual spread grows at higher fitted rents. The Breusch–Pagan test also rejects constant variance (\(p \approx 0.008\)). The model therefore misses by more in the higher-rent, higher-predicted-rent tracts.


7B: The map
The residuals are already a column in an sf data frame. Mapping them is one geom_sf() away.

ggplot(tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = resid_m2), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "grey95", high = "#b2182b",
                       midpoint = 0, labels = scales::dollar) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Where the rent model is wrong",
       subtitle = "Red = rent higher than predicted · Blue = lower than predicted",
       fill = "Residual")








Stop and look: If the errors were random, the map would look speckled. Does it? Where do the reds sit together? What might those places have in common that the model doesn’t know about?
Write down your answer. We’ll come back to it in Weeks 6 and 7.
The residuals are spatially clustered rather than speckled. Nearby red and blue tracts form patches around central and university-adjacent areas and in parts of North and Northeast Philadelphia. This suggests that the model is missing place-based factors such as access to jobs and transit, universities, neighborhood amenities, and housing type.

Part 8: The Challenge
Your team’s job: build the best model for predicting tract median rent, then use it to answer the agency’s question.

Rules

The grade is 10-fold CV RMSE. Use model_df (or tracts) and run set.seed(5080) directly before train(), exactly as in Part 6B, so every team is tested on the same folds.
Don’t drop rows. If you add a variable with missing values, you change the folds and the comparison stops being fair. Fill the gaps or choose a different variable.
You may add any ACS variables (use load_variables(2023, "acs5") to browse) and any spatial feature you can build with Week 4 tools: distances, buffers, counts.
You may not use anything built from rent itself. That rules out med_rentM, rent_cv, rent burden (B25071), and the rent distribution tables (B25063). Ask yourself: would the agency have this variable for a tract whose rent it’s trying to predict? If not, using it is cheating the test. That’s called leakage.

    units_50_plus    = "B25024_009",
    avg_hh_size      = "B25010_001"
  )
)

# Coordinates let the model learn a smooth two-dimensional location surface.
center_xy <- tracts %>%
  st_centroid() %>%
  st_coordinates()

challenge_df <- tracts %>%
  left_join(challenge_acs, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(
    pct_vacant = vacant_unitsE / housing_unitsE * 100,
    pct_poverty = poverty_belowE / poverty_totalE * 100,
    pct_no_vehicle = no_vehicleE / hh_totalE * 100,
    pct_transit = transitE / commute_totalE * 100,
    pct_walk = walkE / commute_totalE * 100,
    pct_wfh = work_from_homeE / commute_totalE * 100,
    pct_large_building = (units_20_49E + units_50_plusE) /
      structure_totalE * 100,
    x_coord = as.numeric(scale(center_xy[, "X"])),
    y_coord = as.numeric(scale(center_xy[, "Y"]))
  ) %>%
  st_drop_geometry()

# Median-impute only the added X variables, preserving all 377 original rows.
challenge_vars <- c(
  "med_home_valueE", "med_ageE", "pct_vacant", "pct_poverty",
  "pct_no_vehicle", "med_year_builtE", "pct_transit", "pct_walk",
  "pct_wfh", "pct_large_building", "avg_hh_sizeE"
)

for (v in challenge_vars) {
  good <- is.finite(challenge_df[[v]])
  challenge_df[[v]][!good] <- median(challenge_df[[v]][good])
}

  med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations +
  poly(log(med_home_valueE), 2, raw = TRUE) +
  pct_vacant + pct_poverty + pct_no_vehicle +
  med_ageE + med_year_builtE +
  poly(x_coord, 2, raw = TRUE) * poly(y_coord, 2, raw = TRUE)

  baseline_formula,
  . ~ . + pct_large_building
)

final_formula <- update(
  building_formula,
  . ~ . +
  pct_transit + pct_walk + pct_wfh + avg_hh_sizeE
)

stopifnot(nrow(challenge_df) == nrow(model_df))

  baseline_formula, data = challenge_df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl
)

set.seed(5080)
cv_building <- train(
  building_formula, data = challenge_df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl
)

set.seed(5080)

  final_formula,
  data = challenge_df,
  method = "lm",

)

    c(
      cv_baseline$results$RMSE,
      cv_building$results$RMSE,

1. CV RMSE. The final model’s 10-fold CV RMSE is $218.22, meaning its typical out-of-fold prediction error is about $218 per month. This is about $34.74 lower than m2.
2. Added feature. I added pct_large_building, the share of housing units in buildings with at least 20 units. It captures housing form and dense apartment markets that the demographic predictors miss. Adding it to the otherwise comparable challenge model lowered CV RMSE from about $229.05 to $222.53; the full feature set lowered it further to $218.22.
3. One coefficient, read twice.

β̂ reading: Holding the other model terms constant, a one-percentage-point increase in the share of units in large buildings is associated with about $4.35 higher tract median monthly rent. Because the data are observational, this is not a causal effect of constructing large buildings.
ŷ reading: For prediction, that same coefficient adds about $4.35 to expected monthly rent for each additional percentage point of large-building units, and the feature stays because it improves out-of-sample RMSE.

4. The agency’s list. The table reports the five largest positive residuals. I would place the most trust in tracts 369.02, 314.01, and 220, whose rent CVs are 6.7%, 1.9%, and 5.1%. Tract 117 is moderately reliable (13.5% CV), but its $1,173 residual is so large that it still deserves review. Tract 332 is the clearest fog case: its 28.0% CV implies substantial ACS sampling uncertainty, so the agency should verify it before acting.
5. Residual map. The broad clusters shrink and the CV RMSE falls substantially after adding housing, commute, and smooth location features, but the map is not pure noise. A few isolated deep-red tracts remain, so unmeasured local amenities and ACS uncertainty still matter.

Before you present, discuss

One of your variables is not statistically significant, but removing it makes CV RMSE worse. Do you keep it? What would your Spatial Statistics instructor say, and why is neither of you wrong?
A council member sees your model and says, “So your model proves that renters drive up rents.” What do you say?
If the agency uses your top-five list to target inspections, whose rents does a model error hurt most?

Discussion answers:

I would keep a statistically insignificant variable if repeated cross-validation shows that it reduces RMSE. The prediction task rewards out-of-sample accuracy; a Spatial Statistics course focused on inference may instead remove it because its conditional effect is too uncertain. Those are different goals, so neither decision is inconsistent.
The model does not prove that renters drive up rents. pct_renter is an observational predictor entangled with housing type, location, and selection; its coefficient is conditional association, not a causal effect.
False positives can direct scrutiny and resources toward residents and landlords in the wrong places, while false negatives can hide genuinely excessive rents. The harm is greatest for low-income renters and residents of high-CV tracts, whose noisy estimates make them easier to misclassify.

It motivates testing robbery incidents and dangerous-sidewalk requests as imperfect neighborhood proxies, plus distance to City Hall; the map alone cannot establish their mechanisms.

title: Assignment 4: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 5: Transforming features
The outcome remains an untransformed percentage throughout. Following the October 9 Week 6 lecture, I inspect the distributions and relationships before transforming predictors, keep the same rows and folds, and compare models by CV RMSE. The required transformations are a log, a squared term, and a categorical variable. Interactions and district fixed effects are additional tools discussed in the lecture, rather than additional requirements in its Part 5 checklist.

5A: A log for skewed robbery density


Show code
tracts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  transmute(`Robberies per square mile` = robbery_per_sqmi,
            `log(1 + robberies per square mile)` = log1p(robbery_per_sqmi)) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "scale", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~scale, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(title = "Robbery density before and after a log transformation",
       x = NULL, y = "Number of tracts")









Show code

m_log <- lm(f7, data = tracts)
log_beta <- unname(coef(m_log)["log1p(robbery_per_sqmi)"])
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m7", added = "m6: log1p robbery density",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f7, tracts), notes = "Compress the right tail; retain zeros")


The raw density distribution has a long right tail, making a log a reasonable candidate. Nevertheless, log1p() increases RMSE from 9.62 to 9.82 points. A less skewed predictor does not guarantee better predictions.
For m7, the logged-density coefficient is 2.490. Holding the other variables constant, changing density from \(x\) to \(x_{new}\) changes predicted no-vehicle share by \(\hat\beta[\log(1+x_{new})-\log(1+x)]\) percentage points. For example, a 10% increase from 10 to 11 robberies per square mile corresponds to 0.217 points. The familiar \(\hat\beta/100\) rule for a 1% increase is only an approximation for log1p(x) and works poorly near zero.

  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(title = "Check the shape before adding a squared term",

       x = "Straight-line distance to City Hall (miles)",
       y = "Households without a vehicle (%)", color = NULL, linetype = NULL)

The flexible smooth departs from a constant downward slope, motivating a quadratic candidate. Adding the squared term lowers RMSE to 9.34 points, 0.28 points below the corresponding linear-distance model. Its conditional distance association is \(\hat\beta_1 + 2\hat\beta_2 d\), not either coefficient alone: the negative linear term and positive squared term imply a decline followed by a rise. In m8, the turning point is 11.47 miles; I check the selected model’s turning point, observed range, and support near the edge in Part 6. The unadjusted smooth above and a multivariable model’s conditional curve need not have the same shape.

Only 23 tracts lie beyond it, so I treat the outer upturn as a sparsely supported feature of this fitted polynomial, not evidence that moving farther out causes households to give up vehicles. The lecture warns that a parabola continues outside the data range; I would not extrapolate this curve beyond the observed distances.

The lecture’s helper pools all held-out squared errors before taking the square root, whereas the assignment template’s caret helper averages the ten fold RMSEs. I retain the template metric throughout the model log and report both metrics above in the same percentage-point units. The difference between them is aggregation, not a change of outcome scale. Model selection reuses these folds, so its reported gain may be optimistic; nearby training and validation tracts also share spatial context. A spatially separated or later-period evaluation would be needed before deployment.
The final linear model produces 7 negative fitted percentages and 8 negative held-out predictions. I leave these unmodified in every comparison rather than silently clipping them to improve the score. A model bounded to 0–100% is a sensible next step, beyond this assignment’s linear-regression workflow.

title: Assignment 4: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 7: Reflection
Robbery density was the most useful open-data feature. Adding it to the ACS baseline reduced CV RMSE from 12.33 to 10.86 percentage points, a 1.47-point improvement. Normalizing by area helps separate incident concentration from tract size. Distance to City Hall then absorbed part of the central-versus-peripheral pattern, and its squared term improved the linear-distance model from 9.62 to 9.34. These features may capture overlapping aspects of density, accessibility, and neighborhood conditions; their performance does not identify a causal mechanism.
The sidewalk features disappointed me. Their initial gains were small, and removing both from the quadratic model gave a slightly lower RMSE of 9.32. Complaints depend on reporting and may add little beyond centrality. Logging robbery density also worsened prediction, despite making the histogram less skewed. This was a useful reminder that a plausible transformation must earn its place through validation.
β̂ reading: Holding the other final-model terms constant, a one-percentage-point higher renter share is associated with about 0.18 percentage points more households without a vehicle. ŷ reading: If two tracts have identical values for the other predictors, increasing renter share by ten percentage points raises the model’s predicted no-vehicle share by about 1.82 points.
The final map still underpredicts some North and West Philadelphia tracts. I would next measure transit service frequency and walking access using historical 2023 SEPTA GTFS schedules, checking archive coverage before using them. Distance to City Hall cannot represent route quality, transfers, or physical barriers.
Finally, the uncertainty plot does not show a simple increase in error with CV: several large misses have reasonably reliable ACS estimates. A median outcome standard error of 5.50 points indicates meaningful noise, but it cannot be subtracted from RMSE to isolate model error. Sampling uncertainty, omitted variables, and imperfect functional form all remain plausible. The 24.4% improvement is encouraging, but reused random folds and a few negative predictions limit immediate policy use.
